claims.text: An Al- and Ti-rich high-entropy alloy made from low-density elements is lightweight.
Processing the alloy under inert conditions produces a homogeneous microstructure.
A controlled partial-oxidation processing step induces in situ formation of nanoscale oxide precipitates.
The induced nanoscale oxide precipitates form a stable, uniformly distributed dispersion.
The oxide precipitates preferentially occur at grain boundaries and dislocation intersections.
Nanoscale oxide particles hinder dislocation motion and thereby provide dispersion strengthening.
The oxide dispersion acts as a barrier that slows oxygen diffusion.
The oxide dispersion acts as a barrier that slows diffusion of corrosive ions.
The combined dislocation-pinning and diffusion-barrier functions enhance mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Relative to the inert-processed baseline, controlled oxidation will increase yield strength.
Relative to the inert-processed baseline, controlled oxidation will increase ultimate tensile strength.
Relative to the inert-processed baseline, controlled oxidation will reduce oxidation-test weight gain.
Relative to the inert-processed baseline, controlled oxidation will reduce corrosion current density.
An overly reducing atmosphere prevents formation of the beneficial oxide dispersion.
Excessive oxidation produces coarse, brittle oxide phases that compromise mechanical integrity.
The beneficial effect disappears when oxidation produces coarse, brittle phases rather than a nanoscale dispersion.
The magnitude of property improvement depends on precise control of oxidation parameters and on oxide size, distribution, and volume fraction.
An identical-composition alloy processed under inert conditions can serve as a control in which oxide-dispersion formation is prevented.
